idiom_name: JComponent + ButtonModel (behaviour) with a ComponentUI look-and-feel delegate (markup)
implementation_notes: Swing's architecture realizes the split at framework level: every component is separated into a JComponent subclass and a ComponentUI (UI delegate) subclass, and 'all painting in JComponent subclasses is delegated to the UI delegate', so the component keeps the behaviour and its model (values, selection state, actions) while the delegate - the consumer's look and feel - supplies the appearance. What replaces a render prop is the delegate hook plus the model: a custom L&F subclasses the javax.swing.plaf.basic delegates, and a consumer can restyle one component by installing its own UI. Keep interactive state in the model, never in the delegate, because delegate instances are shared per look and feel.
pitfalls: UI delegates are shared by the UIManager for a look and feel: per-instance state stored in a delegate leaks across components - keep it in the model.
Existing components keep their old delegate until updateUI()/SwingUtilities.updateComponentTreeUI runs after a look-and-feel change.
A delegate's paint must honour the model's state flags (enabled, pressed, rollover) or interaction feedback disappears even though the behaviour still works.

variants.name: Swing model + UI delegate (ComponentUI): the component keeps the model, the look-and-feel delegate paints

variants.name: JavaFX: Control plus Skin supplies the visual representation
variants.implementation_notes: JavaFX names the same split Control + Skin: a Skin is 'an interface for defining the visual representation of user interface controls' and is installed on and disposed from a Skinnable control through its lifecycle, so the consumer supplies the skin's node graph and CSS while the control keeps the behaviour and its properties. Choose this variant for modern JavaFX code; the discipline the documentation states - a skin should not modify its control outside install(), and must undo those changes in dispose() - is what keeps the separation honest.
pitfalls: A skin must not touch its control outside install() and must undo everything in dispose(), or its changes survive removal and the control drifts.
getNode() must stay stable for the skin's lifetime; swapping the root node invalidates the framework's scene-graph bookkeeping.
Skins are per control (unlike Swing's shared UI delegates), so behaviour placed in the skin splits the state machine across two objects - keep behaviour in the control.
